document.abstract: In this study, we investigate three-dimensional (3D) video technology based on spatial imaging to implement a next-generation broadcasting service. This technology allows viewers to watch 3D videos without the need for specialized glasses. However, the main challenge associated with the application of this technology is the large amount of ray information that needs to be acquired and reproduced to improve the quality of the 3D videos. Therefore, we are in the process of actively developing methods to acquire high-density ray information from multiviewpoint images, captured using a multicamera system; in addition, we are devising 3D display methods using multiple display devices. In this paper, we present the most recent results of our research regarding 3D television technologies, including a prototype system based on our novel display method called “Aktina Vision.” This system can reproduce 3D videos of real objects at a resolution of approximately 330,000 pixels, three times that of conventional full-parallax spatial imaging methods using a lens array.

authors.bio: Hayato Watanabe received BS and MS degrees in information and computer science from Keio University, Tokyo, Japan, in 2010 and 2012, respectively. In 2012, he joined the Japan Broadcasting Corporation (NHK), Tokyo. Since 2015, he has been engaged in research on three-dimensional September 2020 | SMPTE Motion Imaging Journal 7 display systems with the NHK Science & Technology Research Laboratories (STRL).
authors.name: Hayato Watanabe

authors.bio: Hisayuki Sasaki received a BS degree in engineering systems and an MS degree in engineering mechanics from the University of Tsukuba, Tsukuba, Japan, in 1999 and 2001, respectively, and a PhD degree in information sciences from Tohoku University, Sendai, Japan, in 2018. He joined NHK in 2001 and worked at the Akita Broadcasting Station. Since 2006, he has been engaged in research on three-dimensional (3D) imaging systems at the NHK STRL.
authors.name: Hisayuki Sasaki

authors.bio: Kensuke Ikeya received a BS degree in engineering from the Tokyo University of Agriculture and Technology, Tokyo, Japan, in 2004, an MS degree in engineering from the University of Electro-Communications, Tokyo, in 2006, and a PhD degree in engineering from the Tokyo Institute of Technology, in 2018. He joined NHK in 2006. Since 2009, he has been engaged in research on multiviewpoint robotic cameras and their applications with the NHK STRL.
authors.name: Kensuke Ikeya

authors.bio: Naoto Okaichi received an MS degree in complexity science and engineering from the University of Tokyo, Tokyo, Japan in 2008. He is currently pursuing a PhD degree in interdisciplinary information studies with the University of Tokyo. He joined NHK in 2008. Since 2012, he has been with the NHK Science & Technology Research Laboratories, where he has been engaged in research on three-dimensional display systems.
authors.name: Naoto Okaichi

authors.bio: Masanori Kano received BS and MS degrees from Sophia University, Tokyo, Japan, in 2007 and 2009, respectively. He joined NHK in 2009, and he has been working with the Science & Technology Research Laboratories since 2013. His research interests include camera calibration, 3D image processing, and 3D display.
authors.name: Masanori Kano

authors.bio: Takuya Omura received BE and ME degrees in mechanical engineering from Keio University, Tokyo, Japan, in 2016 and 2018, respectively. In 2018, he joined NHK. Since 2018, he has been engaged in research on threedimensional display systems with the NHK STRL.
authors.name: Takuya Omura

authors.bio: Kensuke Hisatomi received BE and ME degrees in applied physics from Waseda University, Shinjuku, Japan, in 1997 and 1999, respectively, and a PhD degree in information science and technology from the University of Tokyo, Japan, in 2016. He joined NHK in 1999. From 2003 to 2007, he worked in the Engineering Administration Department, where he was involved in the development of digital broadcasting. He has been with NHK STRL, since 2007. He was a visiting researcher with Surrey University, Guildford, U.K., from 2010 to 2011. His current research interests include augmented reality and virtual reality.
authors.name: Kensuke Hisatomi

authors.bio: Masahiro Kawakita received BS and MS degrees in physics from Kyushu University, Fukuoka, Japan, in 1988 and 1990, respectively, and a PhD degree in electronic engineering from the University of Tokyo, Japan, in 2005. He joined NHK in 1990. Since 1993, he has been with the NHK STRL, where he has been researching applications of liquid-crystal devices and optically addressed spatial modulators, three-dimensional TV cameras, and display systems.
authors.name: Masahiro Kawakita

authors.bio: Tomoyuki Mishina received BS and MS degrees from the Tokyo University of Science, Tokyo, Japan, in 1987 and 1989, respectively, and a PhD degree from the Tokyo Institute of Technology, Tokyo, in 2007. He joined NHK in 1989. Since 1992, he has been working on three-dimensional imaging systems with the NHK STRL.
authors.name: Tomoyuki Mishina
